method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)' (published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020), 21 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (read at the site-wide licence statement in the footer of https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651) 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice' (published 19 July 2024), 12 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 ('distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-Non Commercial-No Derivatives License 4.0 (CCBY-NC-ND)') (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11365601). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every edition 1.0 claim (S1, LITFL) unchanged and adds S2, a 2024 review of the ESC 2023 endocarditis guideline's main changes (the guideline itself remains unreadable: subscription-only). The WHO AWaRe antibiotic book was checked again and rejected as a second source: it mentions endocarditis only in passing and has no treatment section.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Staphylococcus aureus drives most fulminant endocarditis — suspect endocarditis in every S. aureus bacteraemia and arrange a TOE.** The aortic valve is now the commonest site (formerly the mitral).
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Usual organisms:** S. aureus (MSSA or MRSA), coagulase-negative staphylococci, viridans and bovis streptococci, enterococci, the HACEK group and fungi. **Culture-negative causes** include Coxiella (Q fever), Bartonella, Brucella, Legionella, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma and Tropheryma whipplei.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Risk factors:** structural heart disease (congenital, rheumatic, mitral prolapse, regurgitant or degenerative valves), prosthetic valves (1–5%, early if under 60 days), injecting drug use, haemodialysis, long lines, marrow transplant and immunosuppression.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Half of cases arise on normal valves.** The picture ranges from no symptoms, through malaise, night sweats, anaemia and weight loss, to cardiogenic shock and sepsis; emboli (stroke, septic lung emboli, splenic infarcts) and haematuria from glomerulonephritis may be the clue.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look for** splinter and conjunctival haemorrhages, Osler nodes (tender) and Janeway lesions (painless) on fingers and toes, Roth spots, splenomegaly, new neurological signs, a new regurgitant murmur and left heart failure.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **ECG:** a lengthening PR interval, P mitrale, T-wave inversion or new arrhythmia should raise concern.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Blood cultures are positive about 90% of the time.** Take at least 2 sets 12 hours apart, or enough that 3 of 4 are positive with the first and last more than 1 hour apart — before antibiotics where possible.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **The current ESC guideline (S2) sets a different blood-culture schedule:** at least three sets 30 minutes apart before antibiotics, each 10 ml into aerobic and anaerobic bottles, drawn from a peripheral vein.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Culture-negative endocarditis is most often due to earlier antibiotics,** otherwise fungi or fastidious bacteria; ESC advises routine serology for Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Aspergillus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Brucella and Legionella pneumophila.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Echocardiography:** TTE picks up only about 60% of cases, TOE 90–99%, with specificity around 90%. Look for an oscillating mass on a valve or implanted material, an abscess, or new prosthetic dehiscence.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **TOE is now Class I even after a positive TTE** (to find perivalvular complications and small vegetations), except isolated right-sided native-valve disease with a clear, good-quality TTE; it is also required before switching from IV to oral antibiotics. With high suspicion and a normal or inconclusive study, repeat echo in 5–7 days.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Multimodality imaging is now a major diagnostic criterion,** because with prosthetic material echo misses or cannot settle up to 30% of cases. CT beats TOE for perivalvular and periprosthetic complications; echo beats CT for vegetations under 10 mm, leaflet perforation and fistulae. Enterococcus faecalis now counts as a typical endocarditis organism.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Nuclear imaging (FDG-PET/CT or labelled white-cell SPECT/CT) is recommended for suspected prosthetic-valve endocarditis when echo is inconclusive,** with sensitivity and specificity near 85%; on native valves sensitivity is only about 30% (specificity about 98%).
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **If cultures stay negative,** send serology for the likely organisms and 16S ribosomal RNA PCR on any excised valve tissue.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Modified Duke criteria:** definite endocarditis needs two major criteria, one major plus three minor, or five minor.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Major criteria:** a typical organism in 2 separate blood cultures (viridans streptococci, S. bovis, HACEK, or community-acquired S. aureus or enterococci without another focus) or persistently positive cultures; plus echocardiographic evidence or new valvular regurgitation (a change in an existing murmur is not enough).
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Minor criteria:** a predisposing heart condition or injecting drug use; temperature above 38.0 °C; vascular signs (arterial emboli, septic lung infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial or conjunctival haemorrhage, Janeway lesions); immunological signs (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor); and supportive microbiology.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Resuscitate first,** then IV antibiotics with or without surgery, supportive care and treatment of complications, involving infectious diseases, cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery early.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Empirical therapy, community-acquired native-valve disease:** benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV 4-hourly (children 45 mg/kg, maximum 1.8 g) **plus** flucloxacillin 2 g IV 4-hourly (children 50 mg/kg, maximum 2 g) **plus** a first IV dose of gentamicin 4–6 mg/kg (children: 7.5 mg/kg below age 10, 6 mg/kg from 10).
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Empirical therapy if hospital-acquired, a prosthetic valve, penicillin hypersensitivity or suspected community-acquired MRSA:** vancomycin 1.5 g IV 12-hourly (children under 12: 30 mg/kg, maximum 1.5 g) **plus** gentamicin dosed as above.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Gentamicin:** after the first dose, set the interval from renal function and give at most 1 or 2 more doses, once daily. It is normally stopped after three doses unless streptococcal or enterococcal endocarditis is proven, when it is given eight-hourly and continued.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Empirical cover generally continues for a minimum of 1 to 2 weeks** (home-based treatment is an option for some at low risk); after that, treatment is directed by the organism and the valve involved.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not use clindamycin or lincomycin** — failure rates are high.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **ESC empirical targets (S2):** native-valve and late prosthetic-valve disease, cover staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci; early prosthetic-valve and healthcare-associated disease, also cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci and non-HACEK Gram-negative bacteria; always cover coagulase-negative staphylococci on prosthetic valves. Prefer bactericidal combinations; treat native valves for 4–6 weeks and prosthetic valves for more than 6 weeks.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Partial oral or outpatient therapy is new in the current ESC guideline.** In the POET trial, switching to oral antibiotics after at least 10 days IV was noninferior (primary outcome 9% oral vs 12.1% IV). ESC: do a TOE at day 10 in stable patients; stable, uncomplicated patients may then go home from day 10 of IV therapy or day 7 after surgery, on the same drugs or an oral step-down, with a nurse daily and a doctor one to three times a week.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Not for outpatient or oral step-down:** heart failure, severe valve regurgitation, vegetations over 10 mm, progression or local complications, neurological involvement, renal impairment, malabsorption, or injecting drug use. The patient also needs to be stable with a stable home, ideally a live-in carer. POET was Danish; where resistance is higher, the endocarditis team decides case by case.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Consider valve surgery** for haemodynamic instability, a root, paravalvular or intracardiac abscess (or one that is enlarging), recurrent emboli, or infection with S. aureus, Q fever or fungi.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Operating early (within 48 hours) cut later embolic events but did not change mortality** in the trial the source cites.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Complications to watch for:** emboli to brain, limbs, lungs, spleen and other organs; sepsis with local or metastatic abscesses; valve failure with heart failure or cardiogenic shock; arrhythmias; and death.
claims.locator: Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL); author Chris Nickson, 'Infective Endocarditis (LITFL Critical Care Compendium)', published 29 January 2019, last modified 3 November 2020, https://litfl.com/infective-endocarditis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **ESC surgical timing (S2):** the three main indications are heart failure, uncontrolled infection and prevention of emboli; operate as an emergency inside 24 h, urgently at 3–5 days, or later in the same admission. Uncontrolled infection means blood cultures still positive after more than 1 week of appropriate therapy, resistant or virulent organisms, or growing vegetations, abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula or new AV block.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Emboli and stroke:** ESC advises considering urgent surgery from a vegetation of 10 mm (preventive surgery with no other indication is Class IIb). Do not delay needed surgery after an ischaemic stroke: haemorrhagic conversion (2–7%) is less likely than another embolus. After a significant haemorrhagic stroke, surgery is generally deferred for more than 4 weeks.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Cardiac devices:** remove the whole device when the leads are infected, and consider it in valve endocarditis even without visible lead involvement. If a new device is needed, place it at another site after symptoms settle and cultures stay clear for 72 h or more without vegetations, or 2 weeks or more with them.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Manage through an endocarditis team** (cardiology, cardiac imaging, cardiac surgery, infectious diseases, microbiology). Uncomplicated cases can stay in a referring centre in regular contact with a heart valve centre; refer complicated cases early.
claims.locator: Imazio M, Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine 25(10):718-726 (doi 10.2459/JCM.0000000000001651), 'The 2023 new European guidelines on infective endocarditis: main novelties and implications for clinical practice', published 19 July 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365601/, retrieved 2026-09-24
